# The storyboard

The third stop: the script of the whole page, which the person says yes to. Write it to `docs/story/storyboard.md`.

A plan covers what its asker thought to ask for. Most people ask for the idea and for what moves. Nobody asks what the site does on a phone, or without the 3D, or what a shared link shows, and a script that leaves those out is half a script. So this one has a place for each, and an empty place shows.

## The chapters

A row to a chapter:

| Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What you read | What the pieces do | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## The beats

Under each chapter, a row to a beat. A beat is one settled state of the scene and one block of text.

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Screens:** how much scroll the beat takes. One, or more where the scroll works something.
- **How the pieces stand:** a stack, a fan, a ring, a row, a wall, or what the chapter needs. The same pieces in every beat.
- **What is on their faces:** the person's real pictures and words. Name the picture.
- **What the chapter adds:** anything in the scene besides the pieces. Often nothing.
- **Its caption:** a title and a sentence or two, written from the fact sheet.

A caption says nothing the fact sheet does not say. What a project taught the person, what was wrong before they came, how often a thing is used: those are theirs to tell you. Where you want such a sentence and do not have it, write the question in its place.

## Someone with thirty seconds

Say how a visitor who does not scroll gets the name, what the person does, one proof of it, and how to reach them. The first screen carries the first three. A rail jumps to any chapter, and one link skips to the close.

## Without the scene

Say what a visitor gets in each case. The text is ordinary HTML over the scene, so all of it is there in every row. Say what stands in for the pieces.

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | |
| With reduced motion | |
| With no WebGL | |
| With no JavaScript | |

## The look and the type

Both come from the object's material: plates are ceramic on linen, a status page is dark glass, a paper is white with dark ink. Name two or three looks, each as its ground, its ink, one accent, and the surface of the pieces. The person picks by scrolling, once it is built.

Two typefaces: one for the text, and one for what is printed on the pieces, which belongs to the form.

## Everything else the site needs

Mark every row build, later or never, and say who decided.

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page | | |
| A page for each project | | |
| Every project listed | | |
| How to reach them, and a CV | | |
| What others say | | |
| Languages | | |
| What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | | |
| The page for an address that is not there | | |
| A blog | | |
| A chat | | |
| A legal notice, where their country asks for one | | |

## What you ask for

A yes to the script, or what to change. Give the list of what you decided for them with it.

# Storyboard — Rafael Costa

Concept: **The Weekly Report.** The question: *What's worth doing again every Monday?*
The object: a pad of 8 report sheets — Atlantico, DataTugas, Helix, FraudShield, the Health Data Hackathon, Lisbon Rent Map, Meridian, AutoPilot — the same 8 pieces throughout, never swapped for others.

## The chapters

| Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What you read | What the pieces do | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Subject line | The opening | His name, his one-line tagline, one proof figure, the question | A single sheet, blank, types its header in | Nothing yet — nav rail and "skip to contact" link are already visible |
| 2 | Distribution | Who | Who actually opens his reports: a sequencing core, a bank floor, six teammates, Lisbon renters | The stack loosens; sheets fan a few degrees, each tagged with its audience | Nothing yet |
| 3 | Last week / this week | Where from | The years, employers, titles, degrees, in order | Sheets lay out left to right along a dated line, 2020 to today | Hover or tap a sheet for its title and dates |
| 4 | What changed | How he works | The pattern: find the report costing someone hours, rebuild it — told through the Helix report specifically | The Helix sheet alone turns over, dense and handwritten on one face, clean and typed on the other | A toggle flips the sheet between "before" and "after" |
| 5 | The numbers | What, then what came of it | All 8 pieces of work, each with its real figure or description | Sheets spread into a wall, one project to a sheet | Tap a sheet to expand its description; the Rent Map sheet links out to the live site |
| 6 | Flagged for follow-up | What others say | Beatriz Lima's line, attributed | A sticky note pins itself to the Helix sheet from chapter 5 | Nothing new — the note is already readable without a tap |
| 7 | Sign-off | The close | The answer to the question, his ask, how to reach him | All 8 sheets restack into one pad, a fresh sheet on top, dated today | Email link, CV download, link to the Rent Map |

## The beats

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | 1 | A single sheet, resting dead-centre, blank | Nothing, until the header types itself across it | A thin cursor-blink while the header types | "Rafael Costa. I build dashboards and reports that save people hours — most recently cutting a weekly report at a genomics lab from five hours to two. What's worth doing again every Monday?" |
| 2.1 | 1 | The pad loosens; 8 sheets fan a few degrees apart, still stacked | Each sheet gets one small addressee tag: "the sequencing core," "200+ staff at a bank," "six teammates," "Lisbon renters," "a hackathon team of five," "a study group of twelve," "a telecom's churn team," "a self" (his MSc capstone) | None | "Before it reaches you, a report has to reach someone else first. Here's who's been reading his." |
| 3.1 | 2 (scroll draws the line out left to right) | The 8 sheets drop out of the stack one at a time onto a dated horizontal line, 2020 at the left, today at the right | Each sheet shows only its header: employer or project, title, dates | A thin line connecting the sheets in order, with year marks | "BSc Economics, 2017–2020. Internship in churn analysis, Atlantico Telecom, 2020. MSc Data Science, 2020–2022. Data Analyst, Helix Genomics Institute, Porto, 2021–2024. Product Analyst, Meridian Bank, Lisbon, 2024–present." |
| 4.1 | 2 (scroll turns the sheet) | Every sheet but Helix's stays on the timeline, dimmed; the Helix sheet comes forward alone | Face one: a dense, handwritten-looking sheet, "5 hrs" circled. Face two, after the turn: a clean typed sheet, "2 hrs" in its place | A hand-drawn-style arrow or fold line as the sheet turns | "At Helix he built the dashboard that tracked samples through the sequencing core, and rebuilt its weekly scheduling report. The report that used to take about five hours took about two. He was not doing genomics — he never touched the science." |
| 5.1 | 3 (scroll spreads the wall, then settles) | All 8 sheets leave the timeline and spread into a 4×2 wall | Each sheet now carries one project or job, its real figure or description, and (for the Rent Map) a thumbnail of the live map | None beyond the sheets themselves | Eight short captions, one per sheet — see below |
| 5.2 | — (tap, not scroll) | The tapped sheet alone lifts forward slightly | Its full description, drawn only from the fact sheet | A close control | See per-sheet captions below |
| 6.1 | 1 | The wall holds from 5.1; a small paper note slides in and pins itself to the Helix sheet | The note: "Rafael's dashboards changed how the core plans its week. He is the reason we stopped double-booking the sequencers." — Beatriz Lima, Head of the Sequencing Core, Helix Genomics Institute | A pin or tape graphic | (the quote itself is the caption) |
| 7.1 | 2 (scroll gathers the wall back into a stack) | All 8 sheets lift off the wall and restack into a single pad; one new, blank sheet lands on top | The top sheet types out a final line, dated today | Email, CV-download and Rent-Map links appear beside the stack, not on it | "What's worth doing again every Monday? Finding the report that's quietly costing a team its morning, and getting rid of it. I'm looking for a product analyst role at a product company — get in touch." |

**The eight sheets in chapter 5, each a caption from the fact sheet, nothing more:**

1. **Lisbon Rent Map** — "A map of what a room costs in every parish of Lisbon. His own, live, about 3,000 visitors a month. [Link to the live site.]"
2. **AutoPilot** — "A script that fills in his team's weekly report straight from SQL. Six people use it every week."
3. **Helix Genomics Institute** — "Built the dashboard the sequencing core uses to track samples, and the weekly report that went from five hours to two. Thanked, not credited as an author, in a paper in the Journal of Genomic Methods for the tracking dashboard."
4. **Meridian Bank** — "Dashboards used by 200+ staff. Under a confidentiality agreement — nothing further shown."
5. **FraudShield** — "His MSc capstone: a notebook testing fraud detection on a public dataset of card transactions. Never real-time, never deployed."
6. **Health Data Hackathon, 2023** — "Won with a team of five. His part was the charts."
7. **DataTugas** — "A study group of twelve he started at university, 2018–2020."
8. **Atlantico Telecom** — "Internship, 2020: churn analysis."

## Someone with thirty seconds

Beat 1.1 alone carries his name, what he does, and one proof figure (the Helix five-hours-to-two cut), plus the question. A nav rail, visible from the first screen, jumps straight to any chapter by name. A "Contact" link in the same rail skips straight to chapter 7's email and CV links — so the name, the work, the proof and the way to reach him are all available without a single scroll.

## Without the scene

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | The same 7 chapters, same order, same captions. The 3D wall and timeline become flat illustrated cards — the same 8 sheets, drawn flat, stacked vertically one chapter at a time. Taps replace hovers (the timeline's tap-for-dates, the before/after toggle, the tap-to-expand wall). The nav rail collapses into a bottom sheet menu. One column, larger type, no parallax layers stacked on each other. |
| With reduced motion | Every beat renders straight to its settled state — the fan already fanned, the wall already spread, the stack already restacked. No flying sheets, no turning page, no typing header. The before/after toggle still works as a plain tap between two static states. Scroll moves between chapters with a simple cut, not a slide. |
| With no WebGL | The same flat illustrations used on phones replace the 3D canvas everywhere, in the same order, with the same captions and the same taps (expand, toggle, link out). Nothing is missing — only the depth. |
| With no JavaScript | One plain HTML page, in the report's own order: a header with his name and tagline; a short "who reads it" paragraph; a dated list of jobs and education; a short paragraph on the Helix report; a definition list of the 8 projects/jobs with their figures; Beatriz's quote as a blockquote; a closing paragraph with a mailto: link and a CV download link. Everything in every other version is text first — this is that text, unstyled beyond basic CSS. |

## The look and the type

**Printed Monday** (the one I'd start from) — ground: warm paper white (#F5F1E8). Ink: near-black charcoal (#1B1B18). One accent: a stamp red (#C14C32), used only for the pinned note and for links. Sheet surface: faintly textured off-white paper with a thin ruled line, soft stacked-paper shadow.

**Night shift** — ground: near-black (#0E1116). Ink: cool off-white (#E8EAED). One accent: a dashboard teal (#3DDC97), used for figures and links. Sheet surface: dark graphite cards with hairline borders, as if lit from a monitor rather than a desk lamp.

**Ledger** — ground: gray-beige (#EDEBE6). Ink: navy (#1F2B45). One accent: a date-stamp amber (#D98E34). Sheet surface: cream paper over a faint grid, closer to a bank's own paperwork.

Two typefaces: a clean grotesk sans for the running text (captions, nav, the close), and a monospace, typewriter-styled face for anything printed on a sheet's face — headers, figures, dates — since a report is typed, not set.

He picks between the three looks by scrolling through a short sample, once there's something built to scroll.

## Everything else the site needs

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page (nav rail + skip-to-contact) | Build | I decided — required for the thirty-second visitor |
| A page for each project | Never, for now | I decided — three of the eight have nothing beyond one sentence (Meridian's NDA, FraudShield's notebook, AutoPilot's private script); a dedicated page would pad, not inform. Revisit if he gets real screenshots or a public repo |
| Every project listed | Build | I decided — the form's "what came of it" role needs all 8, not a curated few |
| How to reach him, and a CV | Build | Needed either way — **still waiting on him** for the actual address/method to use, and a CV file |
| What others say | Build | He decided — cleared Beatriz's quote by name and title |
| Languages | Later | **His call** — resume and LinkedIn are both in English; ask whether a Portuguese version matters for the roles he's after |
| What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | Build | I decided — an OG card showing one report sheet with his name and the question; a favicon of a folded sheet |
| The page for an address that is not there | Build | I decided — kept in the form's voice, something like "report not found" |
| A blog | Never, for now | I decided — no writing exists in the material to build it from |
| A chat | Never | I decided — nothing in the fact sheet calls for it, and it adds a thing to maintain for no stated need |
| A legal notice | Never, as planned | I decided — the site is static, with a mailto: link and a CV download, nothing that collects visitor data. If a contact form or analytics is added later, a short privacy line would then be needed |

## Still needed from him before build

1. A real contact address/method, and a CV file to link.
2. A screenshot of the Lisbon Rent Map, for its sheet in chapter 5.
3. Confirms he's fine with the Helix write-up (dashboard-builder, thanked not credited) in beats 1.1, 4.1 and the chapter-5 caption.
4. Which of the three looks — Printed Monday, Night shift, or Ledger.
5. A yes to this storyboard, or what to change.
